title: Unlock Every Room
statement:
A building has n rooms numbered 0 to n − 1. Only room 0 is open; every other room is locked. Inside room i you find the keys listed in rooms[i], and a key numbered j opens room j. Keys can be reused and you may walk freely between rooms you have opened.

Return true if you can get into every room, otherwise false.

examples.why: Room 0 gives key 2. Room 2 gives keys 3 and 1. That is every room, even though room 1 itself is empty.
Rooms 0 and 1 only hold each other's keys. The keys to rooms 2 and 3 are locked inside rooms 2 and 3.
0 → 3 → 2 → 1. The rooms open in a chain, not in index order, so a single left-to-right pass would wrongly fail.

hints: Draw an arrow from room i to every room whose key it holds. What is the question in graph terms?
It asks whether every node is reachable from node 0. Any traversal from room 0 answers that.
Run a DFS or BFS from room 0 with a visited set, then check that the visited count equals n.

explain.intuition:
Each room is a node, and each key is a one-way arrow from the room it lies in to the room it opens. You can enter a room exactly when there is a chain of arrows from room 0 to it. So the whole problem is "is every node reachable from node 0?", which one traversal answers.

It is the same walk a crawler does over the links of a site: start at the home page, follow every link once, and see if any page was never reached.
steps: Mark room 0 as visited and put it on a stack.
Pop a room and look at each key in it. If that room is not visited yet, mark it and push it.
Repeat until the stack is empty.
Return whether the number of visited rooms equals n.
pitfalls: Scanning rooms in index order and only opening a room if its key was already found. Keys can point backwards, as in [[3], [], [1], [2]].
Marking a room visited when you pop it instead of when you push it. That still works but pushes the same room many times when many keys open it.
Treating the keys as two-way links. Holding the key to room 1 does not let room 1 reach room 0.

solutions.title: Iterative DFS from room 0
solutions.idea: Follow keys with a stack, marking rooms as they are discovered, then compare the count with n.

solutions.title: BFS from room 0
solutions.idea: The same reachability check with a queue; the order of visits does not matter for the answer.

followups: Return the fewest rooms you must break into (no key) to reach everything.
You may start in any room you like. Is there a starting room that reaches all others?
